entry.title: Scylla Keyboard Build
entry.content:
3D-Printed and handwired a Bastard Keyboards' Scylla.

Here is a list of materials I used:

  • 58 $\times$ 1N4148 Flyback Diodes
  • 58 $\times$ Gateron Brown Switches
  • 2 $\times$ Pro Micro Dev Boards
  • 2 $\times$ Female Aux Connectors
  • 2 $\times$ Female Aux Connectors
  • 3D Printer Filament

3D Printed Case

The print took ~12 hours total (6 hours for each side) on a BambuLabs A1 mini.

3D printed case, still on the print-plate.

Wiring

I hand soldered each board, this ended being the most laborious part of this project as each side of the keyboard has 29 keys. Additionally, with 3 solder joints (2 wires and a diode) per key, 30 connections to the microcontroller, and 3 connections to the AUX jack, this worked out to $2 \times 29 + 2 \times 5 \times 6 + 2 \times 6 = 124$ solder joints in total. I also had to cut and strip each wire to fit properly into the case.

Keyboard wiring (minus the μC)

Firmware & Keymaps

For the firmware I used QMK, an "open-source keyboard firmware for Atmel AVR and Arm USB families". I had to write my own hardware configuration files to match with my microcontroller and wiring. The documentation for QMK and made things super easy.

For keymaps I have 4 layers, one for typing, the second and third for symbols, arrow keys, and function keys, and the last is a special layer that is triggered when both layer keys are pressed that accesses some system features.

All layers have a transparent thumb cluster.

Base Layer

For my base layer I am just using a standard QWERTY.

entry.title: Solving Cart Pole with a PID Controller
entry.content:
This is my solution to the classic Cart-Pole problem, using a simple PID controller implemented in python and Gymnasium.

Proportional-Derivative Control

For balancing the pole a simple PD controller was sufficient. In my implementation, I approximated the derivative error with a Tustin transform.

PD Controller: $$u(t)=K_p\cdot e(t)+K_d\cdot\frac{de(t)}{dt}$$ discrete approximation, $$\Rightarrow u[n]\approx K_p\cdot e[n]+2K_d\cdot\frac{e[n]-e[n-1]}{T_s}$$

Integral Control

For integral control, I used a backwards euler approximation - where $K_i\int^{t}_{0}{e(\tau)d\tau}$ is the integral term:

$$K_i\int^{t}_{0}{e(\tau)d\tau}\approx K_i T_s\sum^{n}_{k=1}{e[k]}$$

To deal with memory constraints, a ring buffer was used to capture the integral over a fixed range.

Code

Here is the very simple code snippet of my controller logic. $T_s$ and other constants are aggregated into the controller gains and prev_errs is a ring buffer.

err = -obs[2]  # pole angle
err_d = err - prev_errs[0]
err_i = Ts * sum(prev_errs)

ctrl_sig = Kp * err + Ki * err_i + Kd * err_d

action = 1 if ctrl_sig < 0 else 0  # discretize the output

Result

This simple application of PID yields a decently stable output, but I still need to do some parameter tuning especially on the integral term.
